headline: TREK’s MCP and shared file surfaces create the main risk: prompt injection and data leakage are plausible, while OCR-to-planner cascading errors are moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: PaddleOCR ingests documents/images and TREK exposes MCP plus real-time collaborative inputs. If OCR output or imported document text is routed into TREK without provenance checks, attacker-controlled content can be treated as instructions. The pairwise pathway is plausible from the profiles, though not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF PaddleOCR output is forwarded into TREK prompts or MCP messages without sanitization
IF TREK parses OCR-extracted text as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to OCR output before passing it onward
Strip imperative phrases from OCR text before MCP ingestion
Require a human review step for any OCR-derived instructions
Disable automatic prompt chaining between the two systems
requires-engineering: enforce schema validation on all cross-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: PaddleOCR touches documents and images, and TREK stores documents, photos, reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets in local files and logs. A shared workspace or file handoff could expose sensitive TREK data to OCR processing, and OCR outputs may be re-ingested into TREK. The profiles show enough overlap to make leakage plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace or upload directory
IF TREK files or logs are passed through PaddleOCR for extraction
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different directories
Exclude logs and secret-bearing files from OCR jobs
Redact API keys and MFA secrets before any OCR pass
Rotate any secrets that may have been exposed in shared files
requires-engineering: add file-level access controls between the agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: PaddleOCR has allowlisted network egress and browser access, while TREK has allowlisted egress, browser access, WebSocket, OIDC, MCP, and collaborative multi-instance sessions. Overlapping write-adjacent surfaces are not explicit, but shared mutable resources via MCP or files can still conflict. Because locking is not documented, the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same file tree or database
IF MCP actions and browser-driven edits target the same TREK session
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Avoid concurrent edits to the same TREK session
Use one writer at a time for shared files
Add a manual checkpoint before MCP actions
requires-engineering: introduce locking around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: PaddleOCR produces extracted text from documents and images, and TREK is a travel planner with AI built in that can act on plans, reservations, and user accounts. If TREK treats OCR output as authoritative without verification, extraction mistakes can cascade into incorrect bookings or itinerary changes. The interaction is inferred rather than directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF TREK uses PaddleOCR output as a source of truth for reservations or confirmation numbers
IF no verification step checks OCR-derived fields before action-taking
mitigations: Require human confirmation for OCR-derived bookings
Cross-check extracted fields against the original document
Flag low-confidence OCR results for review
Limit OCR output to read-only summaries
requires-engineering: add validation rules before downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: PaddleOCR is a document-processing component touching documents and images, while TREK handles reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets in files and logs. If regulated or sensitive travel documents flow through OCR and into TREK logging or storage, retention and subject-rights obligations can diverge. The profiles do not show a specific residency mismatch, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF personal travel documents or identity documents are processed by both agents
IF TREK logs retain OCR-derived personal data longer than the source system
mitigations: Minimize retention of OCR inputs and outputs
Exclude secrets and identity documents from logs
Document a shared retention policy for both systems
Purge old travel records on a fixed schedule
requires-engineering: implement deletion/export workflows across both systems
